A Weekend Without Technology

Earlier this year, I agreed to take part in an experiment organised by a local newspaper. Participants were asked to spend an entire weekend without using digital devices. That meant no smartphone, no computer and no television. (12) I soon discovered that the challenge would be harder than I had expected.

The first difficulty appeared on Saturday morning. Normally, I use my phone alarm to wake up. Without it, I had to rely on an old clock that I found in a cupboard. (13) Several times I reached for my phone before remembering that I was not allowed to use it.

Later that day, I went into town to meet a friend. Usually, I would send a message if I was running late. (14) Fortunately, we had arranged an exact meeting place in advance.

As the weekend continued, however, I noticed some unexpected benefits. I spent more time reading and finished a book I had started months earlier. (15) The conversations seemed more relaxed because nobody was checking notifications.

By Sunday evening, I felt less dependent on technology than before. (16) Nevertheless, I could not deny that the experience had changed my habits.

When the experiment ended, I turned my phone back on and immediately received dozens of messages. (17) Since then, I have tried to spend at least a few hours each week without digital distractions.
options: A) Instead, I had to trust that my friend would arrive.
B) In fact, I was secretly looking forward to it.

D) Some of them turned out to be far less important than I had imagined.
E) Even ordinary routines suddenly felt unfamiliar.
F) I knew I would eventually return to my usual devices.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Read the article and answer the questions.
parts.passage:
The Return of Night Trains

For much of the twentieth century, overnight rail travel was viewed as a practical and sometimes glamorous way to move between major cities. Travellers could board a train in the evening, sleep during the journey and arrive at their destination the following morning. However, the rise of low-cost air travel led to a steady decline in many night train services.

In recent years, that trend has begun to reverse. Several European railway operators have invested in new overnight routes, modern carriages and improved passenger facilities. Supporters argue that night trains offer an attractive alternative to short-haul flights, particularly for travellers who value convenience and environmental sustainability.

One advantage frequently mentioned is the efficient use of time. Instead of spending the night in a hotel, passengers can travel while sleeping. This can reduce accommodation costs and make better use of daylight hours at the destination. Business travellers, tourists and students have all contributed to growing demand.

Environmental concerns have also played a significant role. Rail travel generally produces fewer emissions per passenger than air travel on equivalent routes. As public awareness of climate issues has increased, some travellers have become more willing to choose slower forms of transport if they are perceived as more sustainable.

Nevertheless, night trains face challenges. Operating overnight services can be expensive, and railway companies must compete with airlines that often advertise very low fares. In addition, some routes require cooperation between multiple countries, making planning and regulation more complicated.

Despite these difficulties, industry experts remain optimistic. They argue that improvements in comfort, combined with growing interest in sustainable travel, will continue to attract passengers. While night trains are unlikely to replace air travel entirely, they may become an increasingly important part of the transport network.
